items.why: The contrast is clear, but the answer simply repeats the opening statement that Jeroboam does not reform.
“Gives the message” could mean the original man of God or the speaker now repeating his prediction.
The closing summary distinguishes those responsible for defeating all four from Jonathan, who kills one.
Connecting the warning with its fulfillment clearly identifies the officer as the person trampled.
Tracking the actions distinguishes the prophet who mounts the donkey from his sons who saddle it.
The two covenants have clearly different parties, though the question uses stiff wording for a direct retrieval task.
The succession is clearly stated, but answering requires only retrieving the event immediately following the burial.
The outbreak of leprosy explains his eagerness to leave; describing the illness also fully answers the question.
The sequence is recoverable, but the question treats the king’s suspected trap as the Arameans’ established plan.
Readers can distinguish the rejected city option from the men’s decision to surrender at the camp.
“Who kills first” turns separate battle reports into an unnatural ordering question rather than testing their substance.
The key “the news” never states that the camp was deserted and rewards an almost content-free answer.
The command “Seize him” clearly targets the man who spoke against the altar, not the king issuing it.
Following “him” back to Uzziah identifies the person entering the temple without requiring outside knowledge.
Following the speaker shift inside the quotation identifies tomorrow as the other woman’s child’s turn.
The question connects reverence with “fear of God” and distinguishes Uzziah’s teacher from his exemplary father.
The officer’s doubt anchors the answer to Elisha’s warning, rather than his earlier prediction about prices.
The stated prohibition explains the refusal, and readers can answer naturally that he is obeying God’s command.
The sequence clearly places talking until daylight after eating and immediately before departure, but requires little inference.
The answer is merely the first action in a short list: assembling the army before marching and besieging.
It meaningfully distinguishes Jehoiada, who distributes the weapons, from David, their former owner.
The final sentence identifies the accusers, but “the addressee” adds unnecessary formal vocabulary.
The first sentence supplies both the son’s identity and the purpose of replacing Amaziah as king.
Resolving “their command” distinguishes the family leaders from the officials responsible for mustering the army.
The donkey prepared for the man of God points to him, but the following “he” shifts subjects somewhat ambiguously.
The officer’s assignment to the gate clearly anchors the pronoun identifying the person trampled.
“You” in the three companies “and you” in the other two “are all” instructed, so the key unjustifiably excludes three companies.
The heading clearly distinguishes sender from recipient, but the task involves only recognizing a basic letter format.
Understanding the rescue identifies “the Philistine” as Ishbi-Benob, not David, whose life Abishai saves.
The men explicitly replace concealing their discovery with a plan to report it to the palace.
“This young man” clearly refers to Paul’s nephew, and either description supplies a complete answer.
The messengers’ return and report clearly precede the plundering, though the task is mainly chronological retrieval.
Uzziah is the clear referent, but “whose love of soil explains the farm work” sounds reverse-engineered from the excerpt.
Linking “my son” to the woman addressing the king yields a clear answer without needing either woman’s name.
The request and its fulfillment clearly distinguish the praying man of God from the king requesting help.
The passage separates three military opponents from the Ammonites, who instead bring tribute.
The city precedes the tomb, but “first” is less precise because the body is initially placed on the donkey.
“Ahaziah’s son’s nurse” embeds the answer in a cumbersome family description and creates unnecessary reading difficulty.
The excerpt explicitly links the city’s calm to Athaliah’s death rather than to the people’s rejoicing.
It distinguishes the two centurions receiving the order from the larger force they must prepare.
The quoted belief distinguishes the hired Hittite and Egyptian kings from the king supposedly hiring them.
Matching “this murderer is sending someone” with the king sending a messenger securely identifies the king.
The following sentence identifies the invitation’s “him” as the man of God, despite the old prophet’s false claim.
Paul’s intended departure is explicitly given as the reason for his prolonged speaking, allowing a clear everyday answer.
The contrast between cavalry continuing and the other soldiers returning makes the pronouns and answer clear.
Tracking “them” through the attack identifies Sceva’s sons as those beaten and forced to flee.
Illnesses also stop afflicting the sick, so ordinary paraphrasing makes the competing answer defensible despite the verb “leaves.”
The plot clearly assigns the commander the task of bringing Paul, while the council must request it.
“Assembling materials” obscures the concrete act of gathering scrolls and makes a simple sequence sound artificially difficult.
The explicit sword order targets anyone following the woman, while her own execution is described separately.
Athaliah hears the noise before going and sees the new king only after arriving, clearly distinguishing cause from later discovery.
Waiting for the commander’s consent supplies the intended answer, but “act” leaves the relevant action unnecessarily broad.
The warning addresses the man of God, but “whose body is warned” is grammatically confusing.
The prophecy’s “he” identifies the future son Josiah, rather than Jeroboam currently standing at the altar.
